text: So far you've inserted literal values you typed yourself. In this lesson, the rows you insert come from a SELECT query instead.

INSERT INTO SELECT replaces the VALUES clause entirely with a SELECT statement. Every row that query returns becomes a new row in the target table. Here, every road-line product from Production dot Product is copied straight into dbo dot LessonDemo.

The target column list and the SELECT list still match up purely by position, exactly like VALUES did. p dot Name lands in ProductName, p dot ListPrice lands in ListPrice. The source and destination column names don't need to match at all -- only the count and compatible types matter.

Because the source is a real query, every tool you already know from SELECT is available before the insert happens. This example filters out products with no color, sorts by price descending, and takes only the top five -- so only those five rows ever reach dbo dot LessonDemo.

This is dramatically more efficient than looping through rows in application code and inserting one at a time. Whether the SELECT returns three rows or three thousand, SQL Server copies the whole result set in a single set-based operation.
Next, you'll switch from adding new rows to changing existing ones with the UPDATE statement's SET clause.
